## Q1
Match List-I (UML diagram types) with List-II.

| LIST-I | LIST-II |
|---|---|
| A. Class diagram | I. subset |
| B. Package diagram | II. relationship |
| C. Object diagram | III. dependencies |
| D. Component diagram | IV. static structure |

## Q1 - Options
(A) A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
(B) A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II
(C) A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III
(D) A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q36

Each pairing follows from what each UML diagram type is used to show.

A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

- **A. Class diagram — IV. Static structure.** It models the static structure of a system through classes, attributes, and their relationships.
- **B. Package diagram — I. Subset.** It groups related model elements together, carving out a subset of the overall model.
- **C. Object diagram — II. Relationship.** It is a snapshot of specific object instances and the relationships (links) between them at one point in time.
- **D. Component diagram — III. Dependencies.** It shows the dependencies among the software components that make up a system.

## Q2
Arrange the following WebApp design layers from top to bottom.

A. Navigation Design<br>
B. Aesthetic Design<br>
C. Interface Design<br>
D. Content Design<br>
E. Performance Design

## Q2 - Options
(A) C, B, D, A, E
(B) C, B, D, E, A
(C) C, D, B, A, E
(D) C, D, A, B, E

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q68

Pressman's WebApp design model organizes design activities as layers arranged from the outermost, user-facing concern to the underlying implementation concern.

Interface design (C) is the top layer, describing how the application presents itself and interacts with the user.<br>
Aesthetic design (B) comes next, covering the look-and-feel presentation built on that interface.<br>
Content design (D) follows, covering the actual information, media and data the WebApp delivers.<br>
Navigation design (A) comes after content, defining how users move between content and interface elements.<br>
Performance design (E) sits at the base, covering the underlying components and infrastructure that make everything above it work.

This gives the order C, B, D, A, E.

## Q3
Match List-I (Coupling types) with List-II.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. Content coupling | I. Modifies internal data of another component |
| B. Control Coupling | II. Pass control flag to influence logic |
| C. Stamp Coupling | III. Uses entire structure/class as argument |
| D. Data Coupling | IV. Passes long list of data arguments. |

## Q3 - Options
(A) A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III
(B) A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III
(C) A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II
(D) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q87

Coupling measures how tightly one module depends on another, and each type here has a distinct, well-defined signature.

Content coupling is the tightest form, where one module directly modifies another module's internal data, so A pairs with I.<br>
Control coupling occurs when one module passes a control flag that dictates the logic path taken inside another, so B pairs with II.<br>
Stamp coupling occurs when an entire data structure or class is passed as an argument even though only part of it is needed, so C pairs with III.<br>
Data coupling, the loosest and most desirable form, is left to pair with IV, passing data arguments between modules.

A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV is therefore the correct match.

(A) Software engineering
(B) Software re-engineering
(C) Reverse engineering
(D) Inverse engineering

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q24

Reverse engineering analyzes an existing system to recover its design, specifications, or other knowledge that is not readily visible. Re-engineering is broader and includes modifying or improving the system after such understanding is obtained.

## Q5
Arrange stamp coupling, control coupling, external coupling, common coupling, and content coupling from lowest to highest coupling.

## Q5 - Options
(A) E, A, C, B, D
(B) D, B, A, E, C
(C) B, C, D, A, E
(D) C, A, B, D, E

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q47

Stamp coupling passes a composite data structure and is relatively weak. Control coupling passes control information; external coupling shares externally imposed formats; common coupling shares global data; and content coupling, where one module relies on another's internals, is strongest. Thus B, C, D, A, E is increasing order.

## Q6
Which cohesions are better than procedural cohesion?

## Q6 - Options
(A) Functional and communicational only
(B) Functional, sequential, and communicational only
(C) Temporal, communicational, and logical only
(D) Functional, communicational, and logical only

## Q6 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q64

Functional cohesion is strongest, followed by sequential and communicational cohesion; each is tighter than procedural cohesion. Temporal and logical cohesion are weaker because they group work by time or category rather than by direct data-flow or a single focused purpose.

## Q8
Match List-I with List-II.

| List-I (software design principles) | List-II (Definition) |
|---|---|
| (A) Cohesion | (I) Degree to which one module relies on another module. |
| (B) Coupling | (II) Dividing a software system into distinct modules. |
| (C) Abstraction | (III) Degree to which elements of a module belong together. |
| (D) Modularity | (IV) Simplifying complex reality by modeling classes appropriate to the problem. |

## Q8 - Options
(A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
(B) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
(C) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
(D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)

## Q8 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q64

Cohesion measures how well the elements inside a single module belong together, so (A)-(III). Coupling measures how much one module depends on another, giving (B)-(I). Abstraction simplifies reality by modelling only the classes that matter, so (C)-(IV). Modularity is the division of the system into distinct modules, so (D)-(II). Option C is correct.

## Q12
Statement I: At the interaction level, components provide an operator display interface and an interface with the communication system used.<br>
Statement II: At the I/O management level, components handle operator authentication, report generator and query manager.

## Q12 - Options
(A) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
(B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
(C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
(D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q30

In the standard layered view of a computer-based system's software architecture, each level owns a distinct set of responsibilities.

Statement I describes the interaction level correctly. This level is exactly where the system talks to its human operator through a display interface, and to the outside communication channel that feeds it data, so Statement I is correct.

Statement II misassigns responsibilities. The I/O management level is concerned with acquiring, formatting, and routing raw input/output data to and from devices, not with operator authentication, report generation, or query management. Those functions belong to a higher level that manages stored data and application logic, so Statement II is incorrect.

Since only Statement I holds, the answer is Statement I correct, Statement II incorrect.

## Q13
Statement I: subsystem models show logical grouping of objects into coherent subsystem.<br>
Statement II: State machine models show how objects change their states in response to events.

## Q13 - Options
(A) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
(B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
(C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
(D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

## Q13 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q37

Both statements describe standard system-modeling views used in object-oriented software design.

Statement I is correct. A subsystem model groups related objects into coherent subsystems, typically shown with package-style diagrams, so a large system can be understood as a set of cooperating parts rather than one flat object list.

Statement II is correct. A state machine model shows the states an object can be in and the events that trigger transitions between those states, capturing how the object's behavior changes over time.

Since both are accurate descriptions of these modeling views, both statements are correct.

## Q14
Which of the following is not one of the principles of good coding?

## Q14 - Options
(A) Create unit tests before you begin coding.
(B) Create visual layout that aids understanding.
(C) Refractor the code after you completes the first coding pass.
(D) Write self-documenting code not program documentation.

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q21

Good coding practice calls for code that is self-documenting through clear naming and structure, but this does not mean program documentation should be abandoned altogether.

Creating unit tests before coding, using a visual layout that aids understanding, and refactoring after the first coding pass are all standard, widely taught principles of good coding.

Option D misstates the actual guideline by pitting self-documenting code against documentation as an either-or choice, when the real principle is that self-documenting code supplements rather than replaces necessary program documentation, which makes it the one that is not a genuine principle.

## Q15
Which of the following is a technique used for component wrapping?

## Q15 - Options
(A) Black-box wrapping
(B) Clear-box wrapping
(C) Gray-box wrapping
(D) White-box wrapping

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q23

Component wrapping is the technique of building an adapter layer around a reusable component so it can be integrated into a new system without modifying its internals.

Black-box wrapping is the most commonly cited form of this technique, applied when the component's source is unavailable and only its external interface can be used to build the wrapper.

"Clear-box" is not standard terminology for component wrapping in this context, so it is not the intended answer here, even though white-box and gray-box wrapping are also discussed in some software engineering references as source-available variants of the same general technique. Because the source material presents these labels loosely, this item is worth a second look against the specific textbook the course follows.

## Q16
Modifying the software to match changes in the ever changing environment is called as

## Q16 - Options
(A) Adaptive maintenance
(B) Corrective maintenance
(C) Perfective maintenance
(D) Preventive maintenance

## Q16 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q23

Software maintenance types are distinguished by their trigger. Corrective maintenance fixes bugs, perfective maintenance improves existing features, and preventive maintenance guards against future faults.

Adaptive maintenance is specifically the type triggered by external environment changes, such as a new OS version or a changed hardware platform, which matches modifying software to keep up with a changing environment.

## Q17
Mr. X designed open source software which must comply with some criteria. Choose the false statement in respect of above.

A. No restriction on redistribution of the software as part or whole.<br>
B. The integrity of the author's source code must be maintained.<br>
C. The software can be sold after distribution.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

## Q17 - Options
(A) A only
(B) B only
(C) C only
(D) All statements are false

## Q17 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q55

The Open Source Definition's free-redistribution clause protects statement A, guaranteeing a license cannot restrict redistribution as part of a bundle or on its own. It also protects the integrity of the original author's source in statement B, typically by requiring modifications to ship as patches or under a different name rather than altering the original files directly.

Statement C is the false one: open source software is meant to stay freely available for anyone to redistribute, not become a paid commercial product controlled after distribution. A strict reading of the free-redistribution clause is actually more permissive about resale than this framing suggests, but the standard classification this kind of question relies on still treats "the software can be sold after distribution" as the odd one out among the three statements.

## Q19
Given below are two statements, one is labeled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.

Assertion (A): Cohesion is a qualitative indication of the degree to which a module can be written more compactly and is able to complete its function in a timely manner.

Reason (R): Cohesion is a qualitative indication of the degree to which a module is connected to other modules and the outside world.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.

## Q19 - Options
(A) Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
(B) Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
(C) A is correct but R is not correct.
(D) A is not correct but R is correct.

## Q19 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** SE: Design, UML, Configuration Management & Reuse
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q81

Reason R actually defines coupling, not cohesion — coupling is the standard software engineering term for the degree to which one module is connected to other modules and the outside world. Cohesion instead measures how tightly a single module's own internal elements work together toward one purpose, so R is incorrect.

Because R is definitely wrong, any option requiring R to be correct — "both correct" and "A incorrect but R correct" — is ruled out, which leaves only two live possibilities: both statements are wrong, or A alone is right.

Assertion A frames cohesion as a module completing its function compactly and efficiently on its own — close enough to the standard idea of a module doing one thing well internally — so A is treated as correct rather than wrong.

That makes A correct and R incorrect, matching option C. Assertion A's exact wording is a looser paraphrase than the textbook definition of cohesion, so if this conflicts with the official answer key, re-check the source phrasing of Assertion A against the original exam image.
